claims.text: Absolute poverty is a lack of income so severe that a household cannot meet its basic needs - enough food, clean water, shelter and clothing - and it is judged against a fixed poverty line: an income per person below that line means absolute poverty.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Relative poverty is a household income well below the average for the society the household lives in, judged against a moving line, usually a set share of average income, so the line rises as the society grows richer.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The test that tells the two apart: absolute poverty is measured against a fixed line of basic needs, while relative poverty is measured against the incomes of others, so a household can clear the absolute line and still sit below the relative one.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Relative poverty is found in rich countries as well as poor ones, since it depends on how far an income sits below the society's average; absolute poverty is concentrated where average income is low.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Unemployment is the clearest cause of poverty: when earners cannot find work, the household loses its wage income, and low pay, often tracing back to a lack of education and skills, holds households near the poverty line even in work.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Other main causes of poverty: large households with many dependants, where one wage feeds many; illness and disability, which cut earnings and raise spending; old age without a pension; drought that destroys harvests where families farm to eat; and distance from jobs.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A cause of poverty can create more of its own kind: job losses cut household spending in a town, and lower spending takes away more jobs, so poverty spreads to households whose earners never worked for the firm that closed.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The causes tend to compound across generations: low income limits the schooling a household can afford, weak schooling limits the next generation's skills and pay, and the two bind poverty into a cycle.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: To redistribute income is to narrow the gap between the highest and lowest incomes, moving spending power from the better-off to the worse-off through the tax and benefit system.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The main policies to alleviate poverty and redistribute income are progressive taxation, transfer payments such as old-age pensions and child grants, a minimum wage, and direct provision of services such as free basic schooling and state healthcare.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A transfer payment raises a low-income household's income directly, so it may carry the household across an absolute poverty line, and a grant tied to school attendance tends to raise attendance as well.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The policies carry drawbacks: as earnings rise, withdrawn grants can trap a household in poverty; transfers and free services must be funded from taxation, which may strain the budget; and a minimum wage a firm cannot cover may reduce the jobs available to low-paid workers.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Illness pushes a household towards poverty from both sides: an earner who is too ill to work loses wages, or earns less where hours are cut, while spending on medicine, transport to clinics and care rises, and where there is no sick pay or free healthcare, savings may be used up or assets sold.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Age can cause poverty at both ends of life: older people who can no longer work lose wage income and may fall into poverty where they have no pension or savings, while young people may struggle to find a first job, and households with many children or elderly dependants have more people to support from each wage.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Promoting economic growth may alleviate poverty by creating jobs and raising incomes and by raising tax revenue that can fund benefits and services, provided the gains are shared with low-income households; where growth is concentrated in activities employing few poor workers, poverty may fall little.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Improved education may alleviate poverty over the long run: schooling and training raise workers' skills and productivity, so they can obtain better-paid jobs and are less likely to be unemployed, though the benefit takes years to appear, must be funded, and depends on there being jobs that use the skills.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
